analysis.one_liner: Slashes power plant nitrogen oxide and sulfur dioxide emissions that cause acid rain.
analysis.headline: The Acid Rain Control Act never got a committee hearing or a vote in the 107th Congress after being referred to the Senate environment committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required power plants to cut nitrogen oxide emissions 70% below 1990 levels by 2007 and tightened sulfur dioxide limits in half, using a tradable permit system with fines for exceeding emissions allowances. It also would have required new mercury controls for power plants and industrial boilers. Introduced by New York's senators, it was sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of areas damaged by acid rain, especially the Adirondacks, Appalachia, the Chesapeake Bay watershed, and New England; people who breathe air downwind of coal plants; and people who fish in or value acidified lakes and streams.

how_it_helps.text: Sets up a nitrogen oxide allowance program cutting utility NOx emissions 56% below 1990 levels by 2004 and 70% by 2007.
Cuts sulfur dioxide allowances in half for 2007 and later years, tightening the existing acid rain program.
Extends emission monitoring to large industrial boilers and requires EPA rules controlling mercury from utilities and industrial sources.
Imposes a $6,000 per ton penalty for excess emissions, adjusted for inflation, plus offsets in the following year.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of large coal- and gas-fired power plants and industrial boilers, who would bear retrofit, fuel-switching, or allowance purchase costs, with some portion passed to electricity customers.

drawbacks.text: Deep emission cuts at power plants cost money that utilities typically recover through electricity rates, so consumers in coal-reliant states would see some price increase.
The allowance trading design lets plants that cannot or will not cut pollution buy their way out, concentrating emissions in some communities even as totals fall.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and ecosystem benefits of cutting nitrogen oxide and sulfur dioxide in half outweigh typical compliance costs, though the tradable system leaves some local hotspots and some rate impacts.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee for the rest of the 107th Congress with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Introduced March 21, 2001, by Senators Schumer and Clinton, and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the same day.
No further action occurred before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of large coal-fired power plants avoided new nitrogen oxide, sulfur dioxide, and mercury limits during the 107th Congress.

for.name: Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Acid Rain Control Act in March 2001.

for.name: Hillary Clinton
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor of the bill.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Jim Jeffords (I-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Coal and electric utility industry
against.role: Coal-burning utilities opposed additional mandatory emission cuts
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory nitrogen oxide and sulfur dioxide cuts beyond the existing Clean Air Act program and backed a competing voluntary approach.

sides.party_line_note: All three Senate sponsors were Democrats; no Senate Republicans cosponsored, and the Republican-held House never considered a companion.

industries.note: The bill would have halved sulfur dioxide allowances and cut nitrogen oxide 70%, forcing costly retrofits at coal plants. Consumers in coal states would bear part of the cost through rates.
The bill extends monitoring and mercury rules to industrial facilities over 100 mmBtu/hr.
